The Keepers of the Eddystone Light

The Eddystone lighthouse stands on a reef of gneiss rocks fourteen miles off the Cornish coast, where the water runs violet-dark in winter and the gulls keep a permanent, quarrelsome parliament. The first tower on the reef was built of oak and iron in 1698, and it stood barely five years before the Great Storm took it, keeper and all, in a single November night.

What replaced it was a tapering cone of interlocking stone, each block dovetailed into its neighbours so the whole structure behaves as one piece when a wave strikes. The engineer who designed it is said to have wished, on its completion, to spend a winter inside it through the worst weather the Atlantic could send — a wish that tells you most of what you need to know about the confidence of the design.

Life for the keepers ran in monthly rotations: two men on the rock, one ashore, with stores landed by boat whenever the sea allowed. Their log books record the small economics of isolation — oil measured in gallons, wicks trimmed by the hour, letters written and rewritten for a boat that might not come for another week. A keeper's entry from the winter of 1882 notes, without emphasis, that the lamp was lit for nineteen hours a day and that the fog signal was fired four hundred times in a single fortnight.

The tower was automated in 1982, and the last keepers rowed away in March of that year. The light still turns, tended now by technicians who arrive by helicopter, but the log books remain in a county archive: three centuries of handwriting, weather, and patience, bound in oilcloth.

Towers on the Eddystone reef
TowerCompletedMaterialFate
Winstanley1698Oak and ironDestroyed in the Great Storm of 1703
Rudyard1709Timber and stoneBurned down in 1755
Smeaton1759Dovetailed graniteDismantled and rebuilt on Plymouth Hoe
Douglass1882GraniteStill in service, automated 1982

Visitors to Plymouth can climb Smeaton's tower where it was re-erected on the Hoe, stone by numbered stone, and read the keepers' names cut into the lantern-room floor.
